Magic Jack

By: Hein Kaiser | Paid

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
we meet Magic Jack who defied the odds of civil war to create a new future in SA

Unique Selling Point:
There are few black magicians and illusionists in South Africa, even less with a back story like Black Jack's.

Summary:
Feel good story about a young man who left the DRC after the civil war to come to South Africa, and learn magic - his passion since he was a young boy, He survived at first selling vetkoek and repairing cell phones on the streets, eventually working his way to becoming an accomplished magician and illusionist.

Further information:
We will revisit his arrival in South Africa, go and see where he used to sell streetside, meet his South African mentor and also perform one or two candid camera tricks on the public at a mall or other venue, possibly even some in the streets of Hillbrow where he started out.

We will speak to him, his mentor and also, of course, publics that he amazed. Also a glimpse of his family life where he now lives, in Turffontein.

Extra Budget Items:
Possibly civil war news footage DRC for cutaways.

It was 2003, and his family had to pack up their lives, belongings and flee civil war in the Democratic Republic of Congo.

After a harrowing journey just to get into this country from the DRC through Zambia and northern Mozambique, Josue’s teenage brother Paul had gone ahead of them to scout for opportunities in Zambia, and he sold copper to send money home.

Everything was gone. The family had to begin again. It started here in 2003, when Josue moved to Turffontein with his family. This spot right here is where he used to sell Amagwenya, and his family still lives in the area.

00:01:57:24 - 00:02:06:07
So while we were talking just now, as we were approaching this point, we had, you know, to be like, oh, the memories are coming back to this spot, right,?

It wasn't as if you just left Congo and came straight to South Africa. What were some of the hardest parts of that journey?

I remember leaving Congo with this hope and when I came, that our life will be better. So that's the first memory that I have. And then along the way, the journey did not turn exactly the way we're told that it's going to be, and we had to lose some other stuff on the road, you know? We became broke along the way because some stuff was stolen from us, picking up money in the streets, some type of food on the street. You can walk up in the morning. You have a beautiful jacket on and you were hungry like what am I going to eat later on? Let me just sell this and you're going to go back home with the house and you'll be like, What happened to your jacket? You were like, I sold it because we need to buy food.

00:03:39:22 - 00:03:45:03
When we came South Africa, I remember I mean, I was wearing slippers. And we didnt

00:03:45:05 - 00:03:45:20
Have any.

Shoes. No, I had no shoes. I had one pair of trousers and a vest.

00:03:50:08 - 00:04:02:01
To make ends meet. Paul worked as a car guard and the brothers performed with a troupe of acrobats. Their tenuous existence was shattered when Paul got arrested and served two years in prison.

00:04:04:17 - 00:04:13:00
Now. It was up to just Josue to fend for himself and acrobatics weren't enough. Neither with a few magic tricks he'd learned from his father as a child.

00:04:15:16 - 00:04:28:16
But almost like magic. A chance meeting with tattoo artist and part time magician Wayne Berger brought him the mentor he had been looking for.

How did you meet? Jesui, a.k.a. Uncle Blackjack.

We go back many years. Maybe 16 years ago. He approached me. Saw me doing magic and was interested. And one thing I must say. But he is dedicated. And that's how we became friends. And we started sharing ideas.

(Kind of open your hand?) Upsound

And, you know, that's something you go to admire. Doesn't give up. He doesn't give up. And I saw that in him. This is a guy that wants to do something. So I'm going to do my part.

00:05:40:10 - 00:05:47:06

00:05:47:20 - 00:05:53:19
I loved to bring a smile to people's faces. And let's face it, Africa need magic right now.
